lessons.title: Click, Whirr: Our Automatic Yes
lessons.key_idea: Like animals responding to a single trigger feature, people often comply automatically when a familiar cue appears, and persuaders can exploit these mental shortcuts.

lessons.title: Reciprocation: The Pull of a Gift
lessons.key_idea: We feel strongly obliged to repay what others give us, even uninvited gifts and concessions, so a small favor or a retreat to a smaller request can win an outsized yes.

lessons.title: Commitment and Consistency
lessons.key_idea: Once we take a stand, especially an active, public, written one, we feel pressure to act consistently with it, which lets small first commitments lead to much bigger ones.

lessons.title: Social Proof: Following the Crowd
lessons.key_idea: When we are uncertain, we decide what is right by watching what people like us are doing, which can be used to steer us and can even freeze bystanders in an emergency.

lessons.title: Liking: Yes to People We Like
lessons.key_idea: We are far more likely to agree with people we like, and persuaders build that liking through attractiveness, similarity, compliments, contact, cooperation and association.

lessons.title: Authority: Obeying Titles and Uniforms
lessons.key_idea: We have a deep habit of deferring to authority, so mere symbols such as titles, clothing and status can push us to comply even against our own judgment.

lessons.title: Scarcity and Defending Your Autopilot
lessons.key_idea: Things seem more valuable when they are rare or slipping away, and like every trigger in the book, scarcity loses its grip once you learn to notice the pressure and ask whether the shortcut is being honestly used.

plan.title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
plan.author: Robert B. Cialdini
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's six core principles, its central examples, and its overall argument in detail; the later expanded edition adds a seventh principle, unity, which this plan does not cover.
plan.one_liner: Six hidden mental shortcuts make us say yes, and persuasion professionals know exactly how to trigger them.
plan.summary: Why do we agree to things we never meant to agree to? Social psychologist Robert Cialdini went undercover in sales teams, fundraising groups and advertising firms to find out. He found that most persuasion runs on a small set of automatic mental shortcuts. These shortcuts usually serve us well, because they let us decide quickly in a complicated world. But compliance professionals have learned to trigger them on purpose. Cialdini names six: reciprocation, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority, and scarcity. For each one, he explains why it works, shows how it gets exploited, and offers a practical defense. The book is not anti-persuasion. Its message is that once you can spot these triggers, you can welcome honest influence and say no to manipulation.
